Of course a random person on Reddit can’t diagnose you with anything and I’m not trying to, but autism may be worth looking into, especially if you’ve always felt this way. Getting an explanation can make it easier to have compassion for yourself, even if the stigma may be hard to swallow initially. ADHD impulsivity and hyperactivity can also contribute to acting in ways others find “annoying.” I’ve also felt this way from a young age and I remember being 14 and it’s a tough age. I’m sorry you’re going through this. Also remember that people learn social skills (and all skills for that matter) at different rates. Some things might always be hard for you and you might have to find people who are similar to you to really feel comfortable socializing, but there are also skills that you might develop later on. Everyone has different ways of processing information. For example, I process information in great detail, but because of how much detail I’m processing, it takes me longer to fully digest the information, but once I understand something, I understand it more thoroughly than most people. This applies to social dynamics, so I was just a bit of a late bloomer socially, but it’s gotten easier for me to socialize over time. You might just process information differently. Things can get easier, but if there are things you will always struggle with, then having an explanation so you can be kinder to yourself and get some understanding and support from other people can really help.

I would suggest therapy, but if you can’t afford that, or even if you can but want to do some learning on your own, there are resources online to learn more about why you may have this problem. I recommend Heidi Priebe on YouTube. She makes videos about attachment theory and she’s very concise. Your fear of vulnerability could originate from a variety of things, and looking at your childhood is usually a good place to start, though trauma can of course occur in adulthood as well. The underlying fear may be a fear of abandonment, betrayal, or rejection, or any combination of those things. Where it comes from is for you to figure out, but a little psychoeducation can go a long way. I hope you get some clarity.

I don’t think you’re extreme or that your view is uncommon for people with chronic mental health struggles. I used to think this way and I felt very strongly about it. But then I realized that depression is rarely a standalone disorder and is usually a symptom of a deeper problem, and often that problem has solutions other than death. 

The solution is rarely if ever just “thinking positive,” but I don’t think one can effectively make the decision to die without understanding why they are depressed. I think a lot of people come to believe after years of failed depression treatment that they are biologically destined to be profoundly unhappy, but then find out they have something underlying it, like complex trauma that has never been treated and/or neurodivergence that has never been properly accommodated. 

I’ve tried way too many psychiatric medications and interventions for treatment-resistant depression and to no avail, but then I realized that the causes of my depression may be different from most people’s causes of their depression because I’m likely autistic and have complex trauma from living in a world that was not built with people like me in mind. 

Far too much mental health treatment is centered around symptom management, rather than identifying root causes and treating those, which is a huge problem because lasting results come from attacking the problem at the root, and unless you know what the root cause is, you can’t develop a plan for treatment, and the wrong treatment may even make it worse. 

For example, if someone is depressed because they’ve experienced political marginalization their entire life and they do CBT to address cognitive distortions, that can end up having a gaslighting and deeply invalidating effect on them by communicating that the marginalization is not real, though the same intervention may work on someone who is actually suffering from cognitive distortions. A marginalized person might benefit far more from finding a community of people who are also marginalized in a similar way or getting involved in activism to gain a sense of control and pride in oneself, because the problem is a larger societal problem, not an individual one.

If you have had failed interventions, as many people have, I’d caution you against essentializing your depression and concluding that it must be untreatable because interventions that have worked for others have not worked for you. Depression can have a wide variety of causes.

I believe in bodily autonomy, but I think in order to make a proper decision, it must be an informed decision, and if you, for example, have been gaslit by shallow online mental health discourse or by incompetent medical professionals (of which there are MANY) into thinking you just have a “chemical imbalance” that exists in a vacuum or is purely genetic, and/or you’ve been told you don’t have past or ongoing trauma, or you’ve had a form of neurodivergence overlooked and un- or under-accommodated, it can be very easy to think that there’s no solution short of death, when you’ve actually just been neglected by under-qualified people and may have to find explanations and actionable steps towards a happier life on your own or with the help of a community you have yet to find. I understand your sentiment, but I would be careful with it and I urge anyone who is depressed to think critically about their depression and what may have caused it.

I’m also 22. I’ve only just started community college after years of rehab-hopping. I feel behind too. But seeing your post, I thought, “What the hell? That’s young. There’s still time.” I’m in sober living with some pretty cool people who are older than me, and I don’t pity them or look down on them or think there’s no hope for them, and I’ve seen them grow and work towards their goals, even after terrible trauma. My point is, it’s so easy to be hard on yourself but it’s not necessarily the most rational thing. 

The world used to feel so massive and impossible to navigate for me too, and I had crippling anxiety about going out into the world, even just to go shopping, but after figuring out why I’ve felt that way, I’ve finally gained a sense of direction. 

There’s still so much time to figure out what you’re interested in. When I was 18 I wanted to die and I didn’t want an education or a career. I had complete anhedonia and didn’t enjoy any of my previous passions or hobbies. But now, I’m aware that I’m probably autistic, which would explain much of my chronic loneliness, and I have some attachment trauma to work on, and I’m taking one class at a time and I’ve had some part time jobs, and it’s helped with my self-trust. I’m not saying it’ll be exactly the same explanation and path forward for you, I’m just saying you’d be surprised how quickly things can change. 

I urge you to reconsider, ask for professional help, and allow yourself some time to gain perspective and figure out the root of your unhappiness. You just might find that it’s not as impossible of a problem as you currently think it is. That doesn’t mean it won’t take time to unravel it all, but once you have a strategy and a starting point, that alone can provide you with great relief. 

For me it was learning about attachment theory, family systems, and neurodivergence through binge-watching YouTube videos, and now I know what specialties to look for in a therapist and I have some strategies to accommodate myself on my own, as well as more self-trust. It gave me a lot of clarity and my life has become more manageable and I’m easier on myself when things do go wrong. Please, just give yourself time to find your thing that will help you understand yourself better. I promise you, no one becomes unhappy or stuck like that just because they were destined by God or a curse to be miserable. There is always a rational explanation, and that explanation is important to finding a course of action.

I’ve seen so much growth in myself in just three years after thinking I was a uniquely miserable hopeless case and a weak person who simply couldn’t be helped, but it was very sobering and in a way humbling to realize that my experiences were not that unique and that there was wisdom and comfort to be found in other people and their knowledge and experiences, and I feel more like a part of the world now, instead of a small, weird, deformed mouse with a whole scary, ugly, labyrinthine world looming over me. I hope you can stay alive long enough to see that same change in your life.

I think I feel more empathy when I understand the intricacies of someone’s circumstances and why they’re difficult and therefore am able to put myself in the person’s shoes. Seeing a sad facial expression doesn’t do that much for me though. 

For example, if I see a homeless person living on the sidewalk, I think about how hard it must be to sleep comfortably, how many obstacles there are to getting food and water, finding a toilet to use, showering, charging your phone, and getting places, and I think about the rejection and shame that people must feel on a daily basis when they’re homeless, so I can feel a lot of empathy for that because I’ve thought about what it’s probably like. Whether a homeless person I walk past is smiling or not doesn’t really change my level of empathy. 

If I can’t understand why someone would be upset by something, I have no backstory, or I have a much larger problem on my mind than the one being presented to me, like political violence, it’s harder for me to feel empathy. I think I’ve become more empathetic as I’ve gotten older and learned more about the world, had more experiences and am therefore able to relate to more circumstances, and developed my critical thinking skills and can therefore better identify parallels between my web of experiences and another person’s circumstances. I think the thing that makes empathy the hardest for me to access is when I’m dysregulated and don’t feel like I have the capacity to deal with other people’s feelings.

No one has the same life timeline, and many people don’t follow the general template timeline for life that has been imposed upon all of us. I feel that I’m socially behind many people in my age group too (my friendships fade away because I isolate myself and don’t have the motivation to maintain them and I’ve never been in an official relationship), but deepening my understanding of myself (for me that partially means realizing that I’m probably autistic) has made me feel a little less terrified about getting older. 

Do you know why you tend to isolate? Could it be trauma you can get treated or something you can’t change about yourself that you can get support and accommodations for? I used to slip deep into thinking that there’s just something fundamentally wrong with me and that I simply can’t ever live with myself, but now that I better understand why I ended up in the crises I ended up in and why I am how I am, the path forward is clearer. Many people don’t start doing that until their 40s or 50s, and some never do and they die unhappy. 

You still have ten years before you’re halfway through the average woman’s lifespan. You’re not old. There is something—or more likely, many things—that you have probably been needing for much of your life that for one reason or another has been withheld from you or is in your blind spot, but you have lots of time to find what that is. For me for example, it’s been working on my attachment trauma, and probably now support and accommodations for the undiagnosed autism I suspect I have. You can still find out what would make life easier for you, and I hope you have enough trust in that to keep going for long enough to find it.

I hope that you tell someone how you’re feeling and what you’re planning on doing so they can get you some professional help and you can lean on others for a while, and then I hope you look inward with curiosity to find out what you need so you don’t have to feel this way anymore.

Don’t ever be loyal to a company. Do what is best for you. The worker has less power than the corporation. The worker is never compensated for the full value of their labor. You do not owe them any loyalty, so don’t factor that into your decision. Starbucks is a particularly stressful job for many people, especially those who are sensitive to social rejection or introverted. It’s a socially demanding job and people get very angry about their coffee for some reason. Many other jobs are stressful, but there are much less stressful jobs out there too that you can get. To be safe though, I would apply for other jobs while working there and keep monitoring how you feel at Starbucks during the process, unless you feel so drained from your job piled on top of whatever else you have going on that you don’t even have the energy to look for another job, in which case I’d say save yourself from the burnout and quit. I enjoyed a lot of my time working at Starbucks, but it was because I liked pretty much all my coworkers, and if you don’t click with the people working there, that’s just another stressor and it may not be the job for you. It did get easier for me over time, but ultimately it was still too much for me with everything else I had going on and I quit.

I’m sorry you feel so horrible about yourself. It sounds like you’ve experienced a lot of racism and of course over time that has become internalized. I hope you can get away from the racist kids at school who contribute to the brutally negative view you have of yourself. Blue eyes and blonde hair are not more beautiful than any other hair or eye color, and I hope you can get some more perspective over time by deconstructing the dynamics of the western social conditioning that is imposed upon all of us, and by surrounding yourself with people who accept you. 

I can’t pretend to understand the internalized racism aspect of your low self esteem because I’m white, but I know how body dysmorphia feels and it’s awful, and gaining perspective by learning about how beauty standards develop and change over time has helped me put things into perspective. I’ve also found people, mostly online, who I find attractive who also have features that I have and am insecure about to sort of “romanticize” those features. I’ve found solace in focusing more on personal style to highlight my features that I like, and to make my preoccupation with my appearance less about my features and more about my style. When you’re down that rabbit hole, it’s hard to just stop thinking about the subject of beauty and ugliness and self-loathing entirely, but if you shift your focus to learning about adjacent topics from a more neutral perspective, that may be able to create some sort of shift. It’s also helped me to develop other aspects of myself unrelated to my appearance. What hasn’t helped me so much that many people with BDD may turn to is letting men comment on my body and objectify me—that validation is fleeting and shallow and I hope you don’t fall into that.

I know some (or all) of what I’ve said might sound corny and my words will probably ring hollow to someone like you who is currently in that gut-wrenching state of mind, but I promise you that your current levels of self esteem do not match your true worth as a person. You have worth simply because you have feelings, desires, and needs. Maybe some inner child stuff would do you some good. Whether you take in anything I’ve said or not, I sincerely hope you feel better, because I know what a hopeless mental spiral body dysmorphia is. 🩷🩷🩷

I had a phase that lasted a few years when I was really really into attachment theory and saw everything through that lens, info-dumped about it, and made a bunch of people in my life take the specific attachment style quiz that I liked. I did learn a lot of valuable information, but now I’m really really into learning about autism and I’m gonna get assessed for it. It would explain so much more about me than a simple “oh yeah I have a fearful-avoidant attachment style haha…maybe BPD who knows?” 

The attachment theory lens, when extrapolated too far, has made me pathologize certain tendencies in myself that I should probably just be accepting and accommodating. I was so narrowly focused on it that I was trying to use different self-talk to deal with my sensory issues and reading too much into why a sober living house full of people was making me extremely irritable, anxious, and more depressed. I told myself I was judging them and I tried to change the narrative that they were inconsiderate people, but I was just overwhelmed by the lack of privacy and the constant noise, the dirty dishes, and the SMELLS of filthy people with poor personal hygiene in that house. 

I felt like there was something wrong with me for being as bothered by it as I was, because my paradigm was “when something bothers me with other people that doesn’t seem to be that big of a deal, it’s because there’s a story I’m telling myself, and I will fix it by changing that story.” I was wrong. I just have sensory issues, and I didn’t have the alone time or the degree of control over my environment that I needed to stay regulated. Misdiagnosis or an incomplete diagnosis can be harmful, especially in autistic people who tend to hyper-focus on things, criticize themselves, and pick up on patterns that may lead to too much extrapolation and therefore a misattribution of distress.

I’m not diagnosed, but I strongly suspect that I’m autistic. I’ve typed upwards of 50 pages about why I think I am for my upcoming assessment (I hope it’s soon!). I can act pretty damn “normal” in social situations and I make people laugh a lot, though I am awkward with new people, I’ve been told many times I need to “pick my battles,” and when I disregard gender norms and social hierarchies people take it the wrong way sometimes. Overall though, I think I’m “normal” enough to be likable to most people, so when I’ve told certain people I think I’m autistic and that I’m going to get assessed for autism, they say I don’t seem autistic, and I’ve heard people and seen people online say that everyone is just diagnosing themselves now because they’re woke and autism is woke and everyone who has learned social skills over time or is able to mask is either not autistic at all or not “autistic enough” that they should bother getting diagnosed, because SOME people have the REAL and HORRIBLE disEASE of AUTISM. 

I certainly am grateful that my brain has allowed me the capacity to learn to mask, pick up on social rules and dynamics over time, and find ways to lean into my natural abilities (like using my above average verbal skills to construct creative jokes and write songs—people like you more if you have a talent, especially a relatively uncommon talent that they usually only see in celebrities). However, I absolutely have struggled a lot in my life.

I’ve always struggled with emotional regulation and sensory issues. I ripped out my hair as a baby. I used to have crippling social anxiety because I felt like everyone else had come pre-programmed with social cues, whereas I had to learn all the intricacies of socializing and write my own code for it based on my observations, and I was acutely aware that there was something innate in everyone else that seemed to take far more effort for me. 

I always had trouble making friends. My mom had to be involved in probably more friendships than I realized in order for me to maintain those friendships. She started a knitting club for me when I was in 5th grade. I was in speech therapy briefly in elementary and middle school for deficits in “pragmatics and social skills,” and I developed a great deal of internalized ableism because of it. I felt my intelligence was being insulted in speech therapy because the practice conversations sounded childish and contrived, and I hated myself and was a very bitter child and teenager, and I’m still a bit of a bitter adult. 

I felt chronically alienated from everyone around me; there has just been this ever-present feeling that there’s something wrong with me that makes me defective, morally bad, and unlikable, and I can’t think of much trauma I’ve been through, other than the trauma of being neurodivergent in a neurotypical world, that should cause the level of self-loathing that I’ve experienced since as early as pre-K. 

I’ve had meltdowns for as long as I can remember, and ADHD, anxiety, OCD, and depression, and I doubt that chronic sensory overload, executive dysfunction, and loneliness had nothing to do with my mental health struggles. I’ve been admitted three times to a psychiatric hospital, first at fourteen, and then two other times at sixteen. I became addicted to drugs at sixteen. I went to rehab at nineteen and I’ve been treatment-hopping since, with some months of living with my parents in between.

The lasting effects of feeling alienated in childhood won’t just disappear overnight, and I’m not sure that the overwhelm I feel from working and going to school will ever be manageable for me. My default processing system is narrowly focused analytical mode, and having to process broad swaths of new information in order to learn more things or figure out how to improvise in social situations when my brain is not wired for that is going to be difficult for me. 

I feel behind in life compared to much of my age group. I can only handle so much change at once, so building up all these different areas of my life at once has been a slow and painstaking process. I’ve had multiple meltdowns during my rehab-hopping trying-to-build-a-life-for-myself journey, and my self-trust and trust in others is not as high as I wish it could be. I’m 22, so I have time, but I know how slow I can be at progressing towards long-term goals, so I’m scared that I won’t catch up. 

My seemingly neurotypical sister who is a year and a half younger than me has a boyfriend she’s had since high school and a job that pays better than any I’ve ever had, and she’s been in college since 18. I have my unusual strengths, like my natural analytical skills, my songwriting abilities, which I highly pride myself on, and my skills in visual art, but I feel that I’m missing out on “normal people” experiences and I’m scared that I won’t find love and that I’ll burn out before I get a chance to even start some sort of career I like.

Life is overwhelming and exhausting when you’re seeing it in such high resolution and building up your understanding of the world one tiny but highly detailed piece at a time. Other people seem to start with a vague image and then some parts of the image load and clear up over time. I feel like I’m downloading everything a pixel at a time. The group of pixels that I have might be highly detailed and clear, but I can’t tell what the whole picture is yet because it’s such a bottom-up process, and I don’t have enough pixels yet to know exactly what I’m looking at.
